lede: Throw a ball straight up and gravity starts taking speed off it at once. It stops for an instant, then gives every bit of that speed back on the way down. One acceleration covers the whole flight, and one sign convention keeps every number honest.

Find a greatest height, a flight time and a landing speed, even from above the ground
Choose the root a height question asks for, and time a fall from the greatest height

md: Once the ball leaves the hand only gravity acts on it, and gravity pulls down the whole time: while it rises, at the top, and while it falls. So pick up as the positive direction and never change your mind: $u$ is positive and $a = -10$ m/s² from the throw to the landing, so one formula can carry the whole flight.

title: Why a negative answer is not a mistake
md: The formulae on the sheet work with signed quantities on a line; they do not know which way is up. Once you fix a direction they keep every sign consistent, so a velocity that comes out negative is telling you the ball is moving down.

stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 16 m/s. Find its velocity 2.5 s later.

steps.decision: Gravity pulls down for the whole flight, so with up positive the acceleration is −10, rising and falling alike.
One formula, v = u + at, for the whole flight: the sign of a never changes at the top.
The minus sign is the direction: after 2.5 s the ball is already on its way down, at 9 m/s.

prompt: Up is positive. A ball is thrown straight up at 13 m/s. What is its velocity 2 s later?
explain: Keep $a = -10$ for the whole flight, as in step 2 of See it: $v = 13 + (-10)(2) = -7$ m/s. The minus sign says the ball is already coming down. Using $+10$ adds speed on the way up; dropping the sign loses the direction.

twin.prompt: Up is positive. A ball is thrown straight up at 11 m/s. What is its velocity 1.5 s later?

optionNotes.why: It lets gravity add speed while the ball rises, which is a = +10 in the up-positive convention; gravity takes speed away on the way up.
The size is right, but the sign carries the direction: by then the ball is past the top and moving down, so its velocity is negative.
It lets gravity add speed while the ball rises, which is a = +10 in the up-positive convention; gravity takes speed away on the way up.
The size is right, but the sign carries the direction: after the top the ball moves down, so its velocity is negative.

md: At the greatest height the ball has stopped rising and not yet started falling, so for that instant $v = 0$. That is the extra fact a height question hands you. With $v$, $u$ and $a$ known, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ gives the height without any time, and $v = u + at$ gives the time to get there.

stem: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 16 m/s. Find its greatest height and the time it takes to get there.

steps.decision: v = 0 at the top and a = −10, so v² = u² + 2as with the numbers in. This line earns the method mark.
Divide 256 by 20. The value earns the working mark.
For the time, v = u + at with v = 0: the same two facts, the other formula.

prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 27 m/s. How high does it rise, in metres?
explain: At the top $v = 0$, as in step 1 of See it: $0 = 27^2 - 20s$, so $s = 36.45$ m. Using $+10$ turns the height negative; dividing by 10 instead of 20 doubles it.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 19 m/s. How high does it rise, in metres?

text: Back to the start: the flight time

md: Back at the level it was thrown from, the ball's displacement is zero again, though it has travelled up and down. So put $s = 0$ into $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$: the root $t = 0$ is the throw, and the other root is the flight time. Rise and fall take equal times, so it is twice the time to the top.

stem: The same ball, thrown up from level ground at 16 m/s. How long until it lands, and how fast is it moving then?

steps.decision: Back at the ground s = 0. This line, with the numbers in, earns the method mark.
t = 0 is the throw; 3.2 s is twice the 1.6 s rise, as it should be.
v = u + at: the ball comes back down at the speed it was thrown, so the landing speed is 16 m/s.

title: Vertical motion under gravity - stone thrown upwards from the ground
why: The same flight worked at a slower pace. Watch where the sign of the acceleration is written down, before any arithmetic starts.

prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 21 m/s. How long does it take to land, in seconds?
explain: Back at the ground $s = 0$, as in step 1 of See it: $0 = 21t - 5t^2 = t(21 - 5t)$, so $t = 4.2$ s. The root $t = 0$ is the throw, and $2.1$ s is only the time to the top.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up from level ground at 13 m/s. How long does it take to land, in seconds?
twin.explain: $s = 0$ at the ground: $0 = 13t - 5t^2$, so $t = 2.6$ s, twice the rise.

md: Measure every displacement from the point of release. A ball thrown from a cliff top and landing at its foot finishes below that point, so its displacement is negative, the height of the cliff with a minus sign. The quadratic then has one positive root, and the ball lands faster than it was thrown, because it falls further than it rose.

stem: A ball is thrown straight up at 8 m/s from the top of a cliff 21 m high. How long until it reaches the foot of the cliff, and how fast is it moving then?

steps.decision: The foot is below the release point, so s is negative. This line earns the method mark.
The negative root is a time before the throw, so it is discarded. The value earns the working mark.
Both a and s are negative, so their product adds: that is why the landing is faster than the throw.
Root the square for the speed, positive on the answer line.

prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 6 m/s from a ledge 8 m above the ground. How long does it take to reach the ground, in seconds?
explain: The ground is below the release point, so $s = -8$, as in step 1 of See it: $-8 = 6t - 5t^2$, so $(5t + 4)(t - 2) = 0$ and $t = 2$ s. Using $s = +8$ asks when it is 8 m above the ledge, which never happens.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 2.5 m/s from a roof 25 m above the ground. How long does it take to reach the ground, in seconds?
twin.explain: $s = -25$ at the ground: $-25 = 2.5t - 5t^2$, whose positive root is $t = 2.5$ s.

caption: Once the string is slack, gravity alone acts: the block rises a little further, then falls.

md: In a pulley question, once the falling block hits the ground the string goes slack. The other block is still moving up, but now nothing pulls it except gravity, so its acceleration is $-10$ m/s², not the acceleration the pair had. Summer 2022 examiners saw many use the old acceleration, or $+10$.

stem: A block is moving up at 5 m/s when its string goes slack, 1.2 m above the floor. How high above the floor does it rise?

steps.decision: The string no longer pulls, so the block moves freely, exactly like a ball thrown up at that speed.
The rise above the point where the string went slack, from v² = u² + 2as.
The question measures from the floor, so add the height it already had.

prompt: A block is moving up at 4 m/s when its string goes slack, 2 m above the floor. What greatest height above the floor does it reach, in metres?
explain: Only gravity acts once the string is slack, so $a = -10$, as in step 1 of See it: $0 = 4^2 - 20s$ gives $0.8$ m more, and $2 + 0.8 = 2.8$ m. Leaving off the 2 m gives the rise alone.

twin.prompt: A block is moving up at 6 m/s when its string goes slack, 0.5 m above the floor. What greatest height above the floor does it reach, in metres?
twin.explain: Gravity alone: $0 = 6^2 - 20s$ gives $1.8$ m more, so $0.5 + 1.8 = 2.3$ m.

caption: Every level below the top is passed twice: once going up, once coming down.

md: **Two times at one level.** Every height below the top is passed twice, so the quadratic has two positive roots. On the way down, or the total time from projection to that level on the way down, is the larger root (Summer 2026).

**Timed from the top.** When the clock starts at the greatest height (Summer 2023), take the time to the top off the larger root, or let the ball fall from rest through the distance below the top, never the height above the ground.

stem: The ball thrown up at 16 m/s. When is it 11 m above the ground on the way down, and how long after its greatest height is that?

steps.decision: s = 11 above the release point, in s = ut + ½at². This line earns the method mark.
Two real passes: the smaller root going up, the larger coming down.
The wording picks the larger root, measured from the throw.
The rise took 1.6 s, so the clock restarted at the top has run 0.6 s.

prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 23 m/s. At what time, in seconds, does it pass 26 m above the ground on the way down?
explain: Solve $26 = 23t - 5t^2$, as in step 1 of See it: $(5t - 13)(t - 2) = 0$, so $t = 2$ or $t = 2.6$. Going up is the smaller root and coming down the larger: $2.6$ s.

twin.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up at 14 m/s. At what time, in seconds, does it pass 9 m above the ground on the way down?
twin.explain: $9 = 14t - 5t^2$ gives $t = 1$ or $t = 1.8$; on the way down is the larger, $1.8$ s.

prompt: A ball thrown straight up at 23 m/s passes 26 m on the way down 2.6 s after the throw. How long after its greatest height is that, in seconds?
explain: The clock now starts at the top, as step 4 of See it did: the rise takes $23 \div 10 = 2.3$ s, so $2.6 - 2.3 = 0.3$ s. Giving 2.6 answers the time from the throw.

twin.prompt: A ball thrown straight up at 14 m/s passes 9 m on the way down 1.8 s after the throw. How long after its greatest height is that, in seconds?
twin.explain: The rise takes $1.4$ s, so $1.8 - 1.4 = 0.4$ s after the top.

Unit 2 sets this as a short question near the start: the greatest height or the time to reach it for 2 marks, then a time to a stated level for 4 (Summer 2023, Summer 2026).
